_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: “He shall recognize” is a separate matter: since “face” is not written there, the forehead counts as recognition.
gershom:a1.1: And if you wish, say: “He shall recognize” is a separate matter. Since “face” is not written there, recognizing the forehead alone is enough for inheritance. And here [for a husband’s death] the countenance of the face is required, because “the recognition of their countenance” is written there.
rashi:a2.1: Gentiles are not heirs: [sons] do not inherit their gentile father once they have converted; [see] the first chapter of Kiddushin (17b).
rashi:a3.1: He did not create it to be a waste: the Holy One, blessed be He, did not create the world to be a waste, but formed it to be inhabited.
tosafot:a4.1: Because in their gentile state they are not subject to inheritance: Rashi explained that gentiles are not heirs once they have converted. But the first chapter of Kiddushin (17b) implies that they are heirs, for we say there that a gentile inherits his father by Torah law. Rather, “they are not subject to inheritance” here means [they are not subject to] the law of the firstborn.
tosafot:a4.2: And he has indeed performed [what makes the world] inhabited: In chapter HaBa al Yevimto (Yevamot 62a) it says, in other words, that even beforehand [as gentiles] they are subject to being fruitful and multiplying. That does not mean they are obligated, for chapter Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 59b) shows that they were not commanded to be fruitful and multiply. Rather, it means that his offspring is traced after him, and that is what “he has performed inhabitation” means here. And concerning a slave it says in Yevamot (62a) that all agree he has no lineage [ḥayis].
gershom:a2.1: In their gentile state they are not subject to inheritance: since a gentile has no [legal] father. Another explanation: as it says in tractate Kiddushin, a gentile [inheriting] from a convert, or a convert from a convert, is [an heir] neither by Torah law nor by rabbinic law, as it is taught: one who borrowed money from a convert whose sons converted with him, etc. That is why he has a firstborn for inheritance.
gershom:a3.1: And he has indeed performed inhabitation: [through his] sons.
rashi:a6.1: One who did not have sons, etc.: I explained it above, at the mishna [46a].
rashi:a7.1: From whom did she give birth: since it teaches that once she came to join the Jewish people she gave birth [to a son who] is a firstborn for inheritance.
rashi:a7.2: Why specifically a convert or a maidservant: this implies that he is a firstborn for inheritance for that reason, because the sons she had in her gentile state do not count.
rashi:a7.3: Even a Jewish woman as well: even if her first sons count as sons, this one would still be a firstborn for inheritance, for the matter depends on the father and not on the mother.
gershom:a4.1: From whom did she give birth: that is, this that it teaches, “once she came to join the Jewish people she gave birth”: from whom did she give birth?
gershom:a5.1: Why specifically a convert or a maidservant, that he is a firstborn for inheritance? Even [with] a Jewish woman he would be a firstborn for inheritance.
rashi:a8.1: Rather, is it not: this “once she came to join the Jewish people she gave birth” does not go back to “one who did not have sons.” Rather, it is a separate case: a convert who had sons in her gentile state and converted together with her husband, and gave birth once she came under the law of Israel; [her son] is a firstborn for inheritance. And this is a refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan.
gershom:a6.1: And it teaches “a firstborn for inheritance,” even though he already fathered sons in his gentile state. This is a refutation of Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said that if he had sons in his gentile state he has no firstborn for inheritance.
rashi:a9.1: Actually, from a Jew who did not have sons: for the sake of “a firstborn for inheritance” there was no need to mention a convert. Rather, [it is mentioned] because it teaches us that he is not a firstborn for the priest, since the earlier sons are called “opening the womb”; and [this is] to exclude [the view] of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
gershom:a7.1: It teaches us: [the printed text reads “Rabbi Yoḥanan” here, corrected in brackets to “our mishna”] that he is not a firstborn for the priest, only a firstborn for inheritance.
rashi:a11.1: This: [the baraita] that teaches “a firstborn for inheritance” is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who counts him a firstborn with respect to the priest, [reading the verse as] “until they open a womb in Israel.”
rashi:a11.3: From her: just as for her the earlier sons do not count, and this one is the “opening of the womb” written “in Israel,” so for him too the earlier ones do not count, and this one is “the first of his strength.”
gershom:a8.1: And he derives: the [male] convert [derives] from her, the female convert. Just as for her, according to Rabbi Yosei, even though she had sons, [her son] is a firstborn for the priest, so too for him, even though he had sons [in his gentile state], he has a firstborn for inheritance. [We follow the correction printed in the text; the uncorrected wording is garbled.]
rashi:a12.1: Leviyya: the daughter of a Levite.
rashi:a12.2: Even an Israelite woman as well: as we said in the first chapter (3b), priests and Levites are exempt.
rashi:a13.1: By their fathers’ houses: from here we learn that the father’s family is called “family,” and not the mother’s family. So why is he exempt?
gershom:a9.1: “By their families, by their fathers’ houses” is written: the father’s family is called “family.” So why is she [her son] exempt?
rashi:a14.1: Who became pregnant from a gentile: since [a gentile] has no lineage [ḥayis] with regard to Jews, the son belongs to his Jewish mother more than to his gentile father; therefore he is exempt.
rashi:a14.2: And do not say [it is] according to the one who says one does not disqualify the child: in tractate Yevamot (45a), where one opinion holds that if a gentile has intercourse with a Jewish woman the child is fit, since we assign him to his mother; and for that reason he would be exempt from the five sela.
rashi:a14.3: Rather, even according to the one who says one does disqualify [the child]: that we assign him to the gentile; even so he is exempt, for he is called a flawed Levite. Since he bears the name Levite, he is exempt.
tosafot:a14.1: In brief: The one who says “one disqualifies [mezahamin]” assigns the child to the gentile father, as Rashi explained; it is called “taint” because gentiles are tainted, as said in Shabbat (146a): when the serpent came upon Eve it cast taint into her, and the taint has not ceased from the gentiles. But [Tosafot hold that] the one who says the child of a gentile or slave and a Jewish woman is fit is the one who assigns him to the gentile, while the one who says the child is a mamzer assigns him to the Jewish mother, and that is why mamzer status can apply to him. Rashi explained it the other way around. Tosafot’s reading is shown at the end of the first chapter of Yevamot (17a): Rabbi Yoḥanan said [the exiled tribes’ descendants] are all disqualified; Shmuel answered from “For he will turn away your son” (Deuteronomy 7:4): your son from a Jewish woman is called your son, but your son from a gentile woman is not called your son but her son. That is, they are not disqualified, since such a child is traced after the gentile mother (and the Jewish women of that generation had become barren). So it is shown there that being called “your son” is what brings mamzer status. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a15.1: On the opening of the womb: for the five sela, [the matter] goes after the mother.
tosafot:a15.1: Mar, son of Rav Yosef, said in the name of Rava: actually, from an Israelite: We rule in accordance with him in Ḥullin, at the beginning of [chapter] HaZero’a (132a), and on this we rely nowadays to exempt from the five sela the son of a Levite’s daughter or of a priest’s daughter who is married to an Israelite.
gershom:a10.1: And do not say: that Rav Adda, who teaches “exempt,” is [speaking] according to the one who says in tractate Yevamot that one does not disqualify the child: that when a gentile or a slave has intercourse with a Jewish woman the child is not a mamzer, since we do not assign him to his father but to his mother; and this one too we assign to his Levite mother, so he is exempt from five sela. Rather, even according to the one who says one disqualifies the child, we still assign him to his mother; he is called a flawed Levite and is exempt.
gershom:a11.1: The Merciful One made it depend on the opening of the womb: [that is,] on his mother, and his mother comes from an exempt tribe.
rashi:a16.1: One who had sons: I explained it above, at the mishna. From the fact that it teaches “she and a priest’s daughter,” it teaches us a novelty: even though he was mixed up with one who is exempt, he is obligated.
gershom:a12.1: From the fact that it teaches “she gave birth, and a priest’s daughter, and a Levite’s daughter,” by inference a priest’s daughter and a Levite’s daughter who gave birth are exempt.
rashi:a19.1: By inference that a priest’s daughter is exempt: and we now assume that “kohenet” means the daughter of a priest.
rashi:a19.2: Badik: he tests us on halakhot.
rashi:a19.3: What is [the halakha]: is her son exempt from [the redemption of] the firstborn or not?
rashi:a19.4: Isn’t this [the case] of Rav Adda: and just as a Levite’s daughter is exempt, so a priest’s daughter is exempt.
gershom:a13.1: And isn’t this [the case] of Rav Adda, who said: a Levite’s daughter who gave birth, etc.? And we established it as where she became pregnant from a gentile. So a priest’s daughter who became pregnant from a gentile is also exempt.
rashi:a20.1: She retains her sanctity: even though she had intercourse with a gentile; and when we assign her son to her, he is like a flawed Levite and is exempt.
rashi:a20.2: From the tithe: the first tithe is given to the Levites.
tosafot:a20.1: One gives her tithe and she eats it: one does not give a share to a woman at the threshing floor, but one does distribute to them in their homes, as it says in chapter Nosin al HaAnusa (Yevamot 99b).
rashi:a21.1: Once he has intercourse with her: the gentile.
rashi:a21.2: She becomes a zara [non-priest]: as we say in Yevamot, chapter Almana LeKohen Gadol (68a): From where [do we learn] that a priest’s daughter, a Levite’s daughter and an Israelite’s daughter with whom a gentile or a slave had intercourse are disqualified? The verse states: “And if a priest’s daughter be married to a stranger [zar]” (Leviticus 22:12): once she has had intercourse with one who is unfit for her, he disqualifies her. And although the Levite’s daughter is also taught there, that is about teruma: he disqualifies her from marrying a priest. But from the status of a Levite’s daughter she is not disqualified.
rashi:a21.3: She becomes a zara: and since she is a zara, her son is obligated in the five sela. Therefore the mishna, too, cannot be explained as where she became pregnant from a gentile.
tosafot:a21.1: But a priest’s daughter, once [a gentile] has had intercourse with her, becomes a zara: even the sanctity of a Levite’s daughter departs from her, and she is lower than a Levite woman married to a priest who was taken captive. That woman, although she is disqualified from teruma, does not lose her sanctity with respect to the five sela. But a priest’s daughter, whose sanctity comes from her own person, loses her sanctity entirely when she is profaned.
rashi:a22.1: This works out well according to Mar, son of Rav Yosef: who explains Rav Adda’s ruling as where she became pregnant from an Israelite; he explains the mishna the same way.
gershom:a14.1: But Rav Pappa, who explained the Levite’s daughter above as where she became pregnant from a gentile, and here cannot explain it as a gentile because it teaches “a priest’s daughter”: how does he explain it?
rashi:a23.1: Actually: the mishna is where she became pregnant from a priest. But a priest’s daughter who did not become pregnant from a priest is not exempt, for we follow the mother only for a Levite’s daughter who became pregnant from a gentile.
gershom:a15.1: Actually: the “kohenet” it teaches is an Israelite woman who became pregnant from a priest. And why does it call her kohenet? Because her son is a priest.
rashi:b1.1: A ḥalal son: he is like an Israelite and is obligated in [the redemption of] the firstborn.
rashi:b1.2: After thirty [days]: [the father] is [then] subject to the mitzva of redemption, as it is written: “And their redemption money, from a month old” (Numbers 18:16).
rashi:b1.3: For his father acquired his redemption: even if the father had given it, he would have separated it and taken it for himself, since he is a priest. And since the father acquired his redemption money, he bequeaths it to his son with the rest of his property.
rashi:b2.1: The father did not acquire: the father was never obligated; rather, the son became obligated after his father’s death, and he must give it to another priest.
rashi:b2.2: For he says to him: this ḥalal [says] to the priest: I come by the strength of a man, a priest, with whom you cannot enter into judgment, for had my father redeemed me he would have taken the redemption money for himself.
tosafot:b1.1: The son is obligated to redeem himself: since the father did not acquire his redemption, the son is obligated to redeem himself even though there is no obligation on the father. So too the mishna that teaches “converted while pregnant, was freed while pregnant.” This is puzzling: in the first chapter of Kiddushin (29a) we derive from the father’s mitzva toward his son, expounding “tifdeh, tifdeh,” that a woman, whom others are not commanded to redeem, is not commanded to redeem herself. So too this son, whom others are not commanded to redeem, should not be obligated to redeem himself! One may answer that this son is not like a woman, for whom redemption does not apply through any father at all. But here, had he had an Israelite father, the father would have been obligated to redeem him.
gershom:b1.1: The son is obligated to redeem himself: for he is like a non-priest and must redeem himself.
gershom:b2.1: Rabba bar Rav Huna said: The son is not obligated to redeem himself, for his father acquired his redemption, and he inherits his father’s property, and the property is exempt.
gershom:b3.1: I come by the strength of a man with whom you cannot enter into judgment: for if my father were alive you could not claim it from him. If within thirty [days], he was not yet obligated; and if after thirty, he acquired his redemption money, since he is a priest. Therefore I, who come by his strength, am exempt.
rashi:b3.1: Converted while pregnant: and she had never given birth before; that child is a firstborn for the priest.
rashi:b3.2: Why? Let him say to him: I come by the strength of a man: who does not heed judgment.
rashi:b3.3: Who has no lineage [ḥayis]: with regard to Jews he has no lineage at all, and this one does not come by his strength, for [a convert] is like a newborn child.
gershom:b4.1: Let him say to him: I come by the strength of a man: by the strength of a gentile, who was not obligated.
gershom:b5.1: It is different here: that is why he is a firstborn for the priest, for a gentile has no ḥayis; a gentile has no [legal] father.
gershom:b6.1: Let him go to this one and he will reject him: the first [husband’s] sons can reject him and say to him, “You are the latter’s”; and the latter’s sons can say to him, “You are the first one’s son.”
rashi:b7.1: It is necessary only: the mishna that teaches “is not a firstborn for inheritance” refers only to the one who comes after him. He himself takes nothing, for the first [husband’s] son says to him, “You are not the son of the first,” and so too the latter’s son says to him.
rashi:b7.2: And this is what it is saying: [he is] a firstborn for the priest, this uncertain one, either way, since he opened the womb and is obligated to redeem himself. And the one who comes after him, [the son] of the second [husband], is not a firstborn for inheritance, for his brothers say to him: that uncertain one is [perhaps] our father’s son, and you are not the firstborn.
gershom:b7.1: Rabbi Yirmeya said: this one can indeed be rejected; the mishna was needed only for the one who comes after him. And this is what it says: he, uncertainly a nine-month [son] of the first and uncertainly a seven-month [son] of the latter, is certainly a firstborn for the priest, since he opened the womb. And the one who comes after him is not a firstborn, neither for inheritance, since his brothers can reject him, nor for the priest, [since he did not open the womb].
rashi:b8.1: And let them write an authorization to one another: the uncertain one and the one after him; each writes the other an authorization for his share, and he goes and claims the firstborn’s portion either way: “If I am the firstborn, give it to me for myself; and if my brother is the firstborn, give it to me for my brother,” for either the uncertain one or the one after him is the firstborn.
gershom:b8.1: So why is neither this one nor that one a firstborn for inheritance? Let them write authorizations to each other, the uncertain one to the one who comes after him and he to him, and claim from their brothers either way: “If I am the firstborn, give me the firstborn’s portion; and if I am not the firstborn, since I am the first [husband’s] son, give it to me for my brother who came after me, since he authorized me to receive it.” And the other says the same.
rashi:b8.2: And if you would say the mishna is dealing with [a case] without authorization: and this is what it says: if they did not write authorizations, there is no firstborn for inheritance.
rashi:b8.3: But we explain it later on as dealing with an authorization: for it says there, “Shmuel said: [they come] with an authorization.” Rather, it must be that authorization does not help at all here.
gershom:b9.1: And if you would say the mishna that teaches “and is not a firstborn for inheritance” deals with [a case] without authorization: but we explain the mishna below, which teaches “if he gave it to another priest, he must return the five sela to them,” as because they come against him with an authorization.
rashi:b9.1: This supports Rabbi Yannai, who said: they were recognized and in the end intermingled: for example, two wives of two men whose children were recognized and afterward became intermingled. Now, when they all come to inherit, their brothers reject them, saying to each one, “You are not our brother.”
rashi:b9.2: They write an authorization to each other: each to the other for his share in his father’s property. The holder of the authorization comes to the heirs of each of the two fathers and says to each, “If I am your brother, give me [my share]; and if this one is your brother, give me his share”; and likewise to the second man’s sons. But if they were never recognized, they do not write, since they never had any entitlement to [their father’s] property. And the mishna too is where they were never recognized, since it was never known which one is the firstborn, and neither of them ever held the presumptive status of firstborn. This teaching of Rabbi Yannai is in Bava Batra, [chapter] Yesh Noḥalin (127a).
gershom:b10.1: This supports Rabbi Yannai: for here this uncertain one was never recognized; therefore they do not write an authorization.
rashi:b11.1: Mishna. Shafir: the actual skin of the fetus.
rashi:b11.2: Genunim: colors. [The Davidson English renders genunim as “pieces of flesh.”]
rashi:b11.3: And grasshoppers: these are not offspring. The reason is explained in tractate Nidda, [chapter] HaMapelet Ḥatikha (22b): “formation” is not said of them as it is of a human.
rashi:b11.4: On the fortieth day: from conception. It is mere water until the day after the fortieth, for after forty days is the formation of the fetus.
gershom:b11.1: Full of genunim: putrid colors, which are not formed into a fetus.
gershom:b12.1: And one who miscarries on the fortieth day: for its form is not yet complete.
rashi:b12.1: One born by caesarean section and the one after him: [who comes out] by way of the womb; neither of them is a firstborn, and the reason is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b13.1: Gemara. We require “and they have borne him”: by way of birth.
tosafot:b13.1: In brief: Rashi’s explanation implies that [the Gemara] derives this from the word “birth” itself. This is difficult, for in Nidda, at the beginning of chapter Yotzei Dofen (40a), [the Gemara] explains that a woman does not observe days of impurity and purity for a caesarean birth because it is written “If a woman conceives and bears a male” (Leviticus 12:2): only when she bears from the place where she conceives; not from the word “birth.” Rather, one may explain that here it derives “birth” from “birth” [a verbal analogy] with that verse, and Rabbi Shimon follows his own reasoning, as stated below, for he includes a caesarean there from “she bears.” And if you say: it says there that Rabbi Shimon concedes that a caesarean consecrated animal is not sacred, because he derives it from the firstborn, where “opening the womb” is written; and the Gemara asks why not derive “birth” from “birth” from a human, and answers that the firstborn is the better source because it shares more features [with consecrated animals: both are animals, sacred, and subject to piggul, notar and impurity]. So here too, let us derive [the human firstborn for inheritance] from the animal firstborn! One may answer that the other features weigh more: a human from a human, and humans are not sacred, and piggul, notar and impurity do not apply to them. And as for the human firstborn of the priesthood, where “opening the womb” is written, Rabbi Shimon cannot derive it from the firstborn for inheritance, since “birth” is not written of the human firstborn who opens the womb. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b13.2: In brief: If we apply “and they have borne him” to the firstborn, it is puzzling. In Bava Batra, chapter Yesh Noḥalin (127a), a tumtum who was torn open and found to be male does not reduce the firstborn’s portion, because the verse says “and they have borne him sons,” until he is a son from the moment of birth; and that he does not himself take a double portion is expounded from “and the firstborn son be,” until he is [a son] from the moment of being. Likewise in chapter Mi SheMet (Bava Batra 142b), a son born after his father’s death does not reduce the firstborn’s portion, from “and they have borne him,” and that he does not take a double portion is expounded from “he shall recognize.” Why not derive all of these from “and they have borne him,” since we apply it to the firstborn? One may answer: were it not that two verses are written, we would have applied it only to the firstborn, that he does not take a double portion, since that is more reasonable than applying it to an ordinary son, that he does not reduce the firstborn’s portion. Proof: for a caesarean, where there are not two verses, we expound it to mean that he does not take a double portion, and not that he does not reduce it. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b13.1: And they have borne him: we require [birth] by way of birth, and a caesarean is not a birth.
rashi:b14.1: A firstborn for one matter: such as this one, who is a firstborn of the womb but not a firstborn among the children, for there was a male child before him.
gershom:b14.1: A firstborn for one matter: of the womb alone.
rashi:b15.1: [Rabbi Shimon] follows his reasoning, for he said: in tractate Nidda, chapter Yotzei Dofen (40a): “And if she bears a female” comes to include one born by caesarean section, that it is a proper birth and she observes days of impurity and purity for it. Therefore for “and they have borne him” too he counts it a proper birth, for we derive [one] from the other.
gershom:b15.1: She bears: “And if she bears a female” comes to include one born by caesarean section.
rashi:b16.1: A firstborn for one matter: such as the second, who is a firstborn of the womb, is a firstborn for the priest. But the first, although he too is a firstborn for one matter, being first among the children and among the males, is nevertheless not a firstborn [for the priest], since the Merciful One made it depend on the opening of the womb.
tosafot:b16.1: A firstborn for one matter is a firstborn: And if you say: for this very reason let the caesarean be a firstborn for the five sela, even though “opening the womb” is written there. For we find at the end of the second chapter (above, Bekhorot 19a) that we learned: [an animal] born by caesarean and the one after it: Rabbi Tarfon says both should graze until they become blemished; and the Gemara explains that he is uncertain whether a firstborn for one matter is a firstborn or not, even though “opening the womb” is written there too. One may answer that Rabbi Shimon’s reasoning differs from Rabbi Tarfon’s. Although it is clearer to Rabbi Shimon than to Rabbi Tarfon that the one after it is a firstborn, nevertheless he holds the caesarean to be lesser and excludes it through “opening the womb.”
